title: Data terminology
subtitle: The terms used to describe data, and what they mean in BDM

There are many terms to describe data. This page sets out what each term means in BDM.

## Raw and derived

Data that has not been processed is **raw**; data computed from other data—summary statistics, scores, fitted models—is **derived**. Reproducible research requires sharing the raw data alongside the analysis code, so that others can replicate the whole chain rather than inspecting its conclusions.

The boundary is less obvious than it appears. In BDM, data stops being raw once it has been processed in a way that reflects an assumption about what the values mean. Filtering out trials with response times under 150 ms, on the belief that such responses cannot be genuine, is such an assumption: the result is no longer raw. Removing duplicate records written twice by a logging bug is not, because no scientific judgment is involved and no information is lost.

The following operations therefore preserve raw status:

- selecting variables;
- renaming variables and enum values;
- converting units (e.g., milliseconds to seconds);
- reordering rows and columns;
- removing duplicates;
- joining or splitting tables.

## Source and tidy

**Source data** is data as the producing system emitted it: whatever structure and file format the task engine, survey platform, or recording device happened to write—structured or not, as CSV, JSON, MAT, or something else.

Turning it into a BDM dataset is a **transformation**: variables are renamed, units converted, columns selected, tables joined or split, and the layout changed so that each row is an observation and each column a variable. The result is **tidy** data. The rules a tidy BDM table must satisfy, and the row and column ordering that goes with them, are specified in [Tables](/spec/conventions/tables.qmd).

Tidy is therefore not simply the opposite of source: it is the *target* of that transformation. Source data may already be tidy, and a transformation could in principle target some other structure.

Keeping these terms straight matters because two distinctions are at work, and they are independent:

| Axis | Question it answers | Terms |
|---|---|---|
| **Interpretation** | Has a scientific judgment been applied? | raw vs. derived |
| **Structure** | Has it been transformed into a target structure? | source vs. tidy |

The two can vary separately. Source data often contains derived values—a total score stored alongside the individual responses—so *source* does not imply *raw*. Transforming source data into tidy tables preserves raw status, since none of the operations listed above involves a judgment about what the values mean.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
Neighbouring fields use narrower words for parts of this. In the tidyverse and pandas, *reshaping* (or *pivoting*) means changing a table's layout between wide and long form without altering any values—one step of the transformation described here, not the whole of it. In data-pipeline vocabulary, *extract* and *transform* name separate stages: getting data out of the source system, and changing it once out.
:::



## Database and dataset

A [**database**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Database) is a collection of data managed by a database management system, implying ongoing interaction: users read and write to it.

A [**dataset**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_set) also contains data, but it also comprises metadata and supporting information. It is a **complete and meaningful unit**: everything needed to interpret the data--including what the measurements mean, what instruments were used, in what context the data was collected.  BDM describes datasets in this sense—which is why the [folder structure](/spec/conventions/folder-structure.qmd) has a place for the design and the instruments alongside the data, and why every file states its own scope.

## Data catalogs

A **data catalog** is an inventory of datasets: it holds, for each one, the metadata needed to find it and to judge whether it is worth obtaining—what it contains, who produced it, under what licence, with which instruments and population—without holding the data itself.

The distinction matters because the two answer different questions. A dataset answers *what happened in this study*; a catalog answers *which studies exist and which of them are relevant to me*. A catalog therefore describes datasets from the outside, and its entries are deliberately shallow: enough to search and filter, not enough to analyze.

Cataloging is a separate concern from the data model, and in the Behaverse ecosystem it is a separate schema—[`catalog`](https://behaverse.org/schemas/catalog), a metadata schema for thematic catalogs of cognitive science datasets. A well-formed [dataset card](/spec/dataset-cards.qmd) is what makes a BDM dataset catalogable: the fields a catalog needs are already there, so listing a dataset is a matter of harvesting its metadata rather than describing it again.


## Storage architectures

A [**data lake**](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/DataLake.html) is an unstructured collection of data from many sources. It is maximally flexible—tables in any format, images, text—which is also its weakness: without structure it degrades into a data swamp.

A **data warehouse** organizes incoming data consistently before storing it (schema-on-write), so its contents are ready for analysis. The cost is that everything must be shaped on the way in.

A **data lakehouse** combines the two: the flexibility of a lake with a semi-structured layer applied on read, giving quick access without demanding that every source be normalized up front. This is the architecture BDM is designed for, and the reasoning is developed in [Design process](design-process.qmd).

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
A [**data mart**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_mart) is a subset or view of a warehouse, optimized for a particular use or audience.
:::

## What to store, and what to share

More data is stored than shared. A study may hold participants' contact details or hardware parameters that will never be published.

What to *store* depends on the study, subject to two constraints: participants must be informed what is collected, and collection must follow the applicable regulations. Being parsimonious with personal data is generally wise (see [Datensparsamkeit](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/Datensparsamkeit.html)).

What to *share* is a different question. In BDM, source data should not be shared when better-structured data can be extracted from it, for three reasons:

- **Usability.** Source data is often messy, sometimes in proprietary formats, and poorly documented.
- **Privacy.** Source data may contain personal information the sharer is unaware of—full names, IP addresses. Defining what will be shared, and extracting only that, avoids accidental disclosure.
- **Responsibility.** Preparing usable data from a source recording is the data engineer's job, not the analyst's. Handing over both the source data and the transformed data transfers that responsibility: an analyst who can see the preprocessing code becomes accountable for errors in it. This does not remove the obligation to verify the transformation—it places that obligation with the party doing it.

In short: do not share unstructured source data. Share well-documented, well-structured raw data.

## Versioning

Datasets change as data is added and errors are corrected, so they need versions. Appending version labels to filenames raises more questions than it answers—whether to relabel every file, only changed files, or only the root—so BDM records the version in the dataset's metadata instead, where [schema.org](https://schema.org) and [CalVer](https://calver.org) provide the vocabulary and platforms such as [Zenodo](https://zenodo.org/) display it. For tracking the data itself across versions, [DVC](https://dvc.org/) is a reasonable choice.

See [Dataset cards](/spec/dataset-cards.qmd) for where the version is recorded.
